label: ECM
rationale: Dave Holland's debut as a leader and the only recorded meeting of Sam Rivers and Anthony Braxton — two of the music's most original saxophonists — over six Holland originals. A definitive 'time, no changes' open-form statement that bridges 1960s free improvising discipline with a swinging, melodic accessibility AllMusic calls 'one of the most varied and accessible introductions to the style one could hope for.' Penguin Guide Core Collection, Down Beat five stars. Essential bridge from the composed canon into the avant-garde.
scope_flag: ECM-label release on the free-jazz/avant-garde seam; pianoless quartet of Circle alumni plus Sam Rivers
bridge_case: For a listener coming from the composed canon: all six pieces are Holland compositions with stated themes that set key, tempo, and mood — improvisation stays tethered to melodic foundations with swinging bass-led time, so the freedom is audible as dialogue rather than noise. The flute-feature title track is a gentle entry point; 'Q & A' shows group improvisation as conversation.

ballot.album: Dave Holland — Conference of the Birds (1972)

scope_check.boundary_note: Recorded in 1972 and released in 1973, it is within the 1940–1979 window, but it enters through the opened free-jazz/avant-garde gate and is also an ECM release; the substantive question is whether its structured, swinging open form bridges the canon's post-bebop center.

ballot.case_for: The dossier reports Penguin Guide Core Collection status and a DownBeat five-star rating, while AllMusic calls it one of the most varied and accessible introductions to avant-garde jazz (S2). Holland's six compositions give the pianoless quartet thematic anchors and swinging, bass-led motion, making the album a credible bridge for listeners moving from composed post-bop into open-form improvisation. The singular meeting of Sam Rivers and Anthony Braxton, alongside Holland and Barry Altschul's Circle lineage, gives the session exceptional gravity and captures a major 1970s avant-garde network (S1-S4).
ballot.case_against: The record remains a demanding free-jazz date: after its heads, the music often abandons conventional harmonic changes for jagged, polyphonic reed interplay, and the absence of a chordal instrument can make that freedom especially stark for a listener whose taste is still uncertain about the idiom. Within a limited free-jazz intake, Coleman and Dolphy records have stronger direct canon consensus and lineage, so Holland's album may be a gateway rather than an indispensable first-tier representative. The Penguin and DownBeat claims are asserted in the dossier but are not represented by discrete source entries, leaving the strongest consensus evidence less auditable than the otherwise solid recording and personnel documentation.
ballot.disagreement: Both references agree that the album should be a scope_call because of the opened free-jazz gate, but they differ on urgency: one rates it strong because of competition from more canonical free-jazz landmarks and John's stated taste calibration, while the other rates it must_have as an unusually accessible and foundational bridge. They also differ on scope emphasis: one treats ECM as incidental and free jazz as the real boundary, while the other regards both gates as active.
ballot.recommendation: John should give this a high-priority ruling as a free-jazz bridge, with inclusion favored if the album's accessibility and Holland-Circle lineage outweigh the gate and taste concerns.
